Criticising all political parties is important, and nobody should be above scrutiny. author: @harshkumar-pi2yg
text:
Sarthak bhai, I regularly watch all your Sunday Show videos, and most of the time, I agree with the points you make. However, regarding your point about the Raksha Bandhan ad, I don't think I completely agree with your perspective.
In my opinion, the boy/brother shown in the ad is wearing ethnic clothing traditionally associated with Raksha Bandhan—proper kurta and pyjama. He isn't wearing shorts or anything inappropriate. So my question is: why should we sexualize or overanalyse the clothes of the woman in a traditional setting? I don't think there is any need for that.
Personally, I have no problem with a woman wearing whatever she wants. If someone wants to wear a bikini or any other type of clothing at a party or elsewhere, that's their personal choice. But when it comes to traditional festivals, religious places, or cultural occasions, I feel it is reasonable to expect clothing that reflects the tradition and the occasion.
I completely agree that ultimately, what someone wears is their personal choice. But an advertisement is created for a general audience, and the creators usually try to make it relatable to the majority of people. Raksha Bandhan is traditionally a festival celebrating the bond between a brother and sister, and for many people, it is also a culturally significant and sacred occasion. Generally, brothers and sisters wouldn't dress in or perceive each other through clothing that might be considered more revealing in such a context. So I personally don't understand why the advertisement chose to portray it that way.
I don't have a problem with the same kind of clothing being shown in movies, parties, or other contexts. My point is specifically about the setting and the occasion. When you're portraying a traditional festival or cultural practice, I feel the advertisement should respect and reflect the cultural context.
That's just my personal opinion. I respect that others may see it differently, but I felt the ad wasn't particularly appropriate for a Raksha Bandhan-themed advertisement.

author: @AyanSohail-oq7vk
text:
My POV on the burqa/hijab: I don't think it's fair to automatically call hijab or burqa “patriarchal” or oppressive just because a woman covers her body. In Islam, modesty and veiling come from religious teachings, and many Muslim women genuinely choose hijab because they believe it is a religious obligation and part of their faith.

I also think we need to separate personal choice from legal enforcement. If a woman willingly wears hijab because she believes Allah has commanded it, that is a religious choice. But if a state legally forces her to wear it, then she does not have unrestricted freedom of dress. I can personally believe in Sharia-based governance while still acknowledging that such a system places legal restrictions on individual choices in public.

What I disagree with is the idea that women's empowerment should be measured by how much of their body they can reveal. To me, real empowerment is being educated, working, earning, creating, making decisions, and being valued for your intelligence and abilities rather than primarily for your appearance.

Attention is also not the same as empowerment. A woman receiving more attention because of her body does not automatically mean she has more power. Research on sexual objectification shows that reducing women to appearance or sexual attractiveness can affect how their competence is perceived.

So I don't think the issue should be “hijab = oppression” or “revealing clothes = empowerment.” A woman wearing hijab isn't automatically oppressed, just as a woman who doesn't wear it isn't automatically empowered. We should be careful not to define a woman's freedom or value by how much of her body she shows.

I wanted to put out this opinion about that Apoorva Makhija thing you said. Although pehli cheez naa mujhe uski existence aur naa use meri existence se farak padega.

But I've been thinking about this whole women empowerment thing lately. First off, let me be clear I do support equal rights, equal opportunities and wherever whoever is best must get the opportunity to perform.

And feminism was started by professors and learned people of their own time in 1970s from what I know about, but lately I don't know from when it has been hijacked by stupid people who have equated freedom = sexual representation only. Somehow, it all feels the same to me now. I could be wrong, yes, but the "influencers" who say You Go Girl and all those things without talking about the nitty gritties of situation that what they are talking about is even right or wrong bothers me a lot. The other day, I saw a video of the mentioned Rebel Kid saying in some interview that if men are stupid enough to pay, you should monetize your sexuality. And yes, one can argue that she is correct, par behen(and not just her) hazaaro careers hain, ye sab hi kyun baar baar sunne ko milta rehta hai kuch naa kuch sexuality related, either via some influencers or media/shows/TV ki bas ye karlo life jhingalala. And audience should try to understand this as well, agar wo normal baatein karegi ya koi bhi so called influencer kuch shocking nahin bolega to views nahin aayenge aur ghar nahin chalega unka, wo baat alag hai ki wo influencer kisi businessman/rich person ka beta/beti ho. Their job is to influence to make money, isiliye imo we should try(cannot 100% succeed, kyunki insaan ho) to collect honest information (jaise sarthak bhaai ke show se 😁😅) and make our own opinions most of the time.

That's why imo, You Go Girl bina samjhe ki wo cheez larger context/long term mein sahi hai ya galat nahin bolna chahiye, warna aise to You Go Boy bolke domestic violence ko badhawa dete aayein hain log aaj tak.

And I get the character assassination part, jab sahi mein koi 2 kaudi ke vyakti ko kisi successful aurat ko neecha dikhaana hota hai to they go on their character which is utterly wrong and I myself condemn it and it shouldn't happen.

But why something always relating to clothes, sexuality and this stupid non sense. The first programmer was a woman, Madam Curie was a great scientist, aisi cheezon ke baare mein mainstream mein baat kyun nahin hua karti 80-90% of the time ki ladkiyaan aage badhe aur badh chadhkar bhaag le in sab cheezon mein. Sports ho gaye, academics ho gaya aur kai cheezein hai.

This is more of a rant which I've felt regarding this female empowerment always getting somehow related to, in a highlighted manner, to sexuality and freedom of wearing clothes and shit. Par ho ye bhi sakta hai ki meri feed hi faaltu ho, although I refrain from watching female empowerment content altogether to keep my mind sane and believe in real equality for women in any field and not go into that factory of brainwashing ki bas freedom matlab sexualise hona. They are humans too and have a lot of aspects to their lives. And for the ones which actually matter, we must fight for it and get them the rights.
